standard.title: Compare ideas across texts using comprehension strategies
standard.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning and inferring to compare and contrast ideas and opinions in and between texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students use comprehension strategies including inferring to analyse and summarise information and ideas (AC9E7LY05). They have not yet deployed strategies specifically to compare and contrast ideas and opinions across multiple texts simultaneously.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use comprehension strategies to compare and contrast ideas and opinions in and between texts.

nodes.label: Comprehension strategies for comparison
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and apply comprehension strategies specifically for the purpose of comparing ideas and opinions within and across texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply at least two comprehension strategies (e.g. summarising, questioning, inferring) to compare ideas or opinions in two texts, explaining how each strategy supported the comparison.
nodes.typical_width: Apply a range of comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning and inferring — to compare and contrast visual representations, print and digital sources, and current event representations.
wider: Develop a comparison protocol: which strategies are most useful for comparing visual versus verbal texts, and why?
Apply comprehension strategies to compare texts with conflicting interpretations of the same event, evaluating the quality of the evidence each presents

response_modes.reason: Students often default to one or two favoured comprehension strategies. Building a full repertoire of all seven named strategies — and matching strategy to comparison purpose — expands the analytical toolkit for cross-text comparison.

success_criteria: Student applies at least two named comprehension strategies and explains how each supported comparison
Student identifies at least one similarity and one difference between ideas or opinions in the texts compared
nodes.hinge_reason: Cross-text comparison at N2 depends on being able to deploy multiple strategies flexibly — students defaulting to one strategy produce shallow comparisons that miss the multiple dimensions needed for the descriptor's comparison task.

nodes.label: Comparing and contrasting across texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare and contrast ideas and opinions in and between texts, identifying positions, evaluating evidence and summarising the relationship between them.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare ideas or opinions from two texts on the same topic, identifying how they are similar, how they differ, and what the difference reveals about the texts' positions.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and contrast representations of an event in print and digital sources — summarising qualities, identifying opinions and analysing evidence — and compare articles representing a current event, contrasting ideas and opinions across texts.
wider: Compare visual representations of the same issue across online news sources and evaluate how the visual choices support or contradict the verbal argument
Compare three or more texts on the same issue and map the ideological positions they represent — evaluating whether any positions are absent

response_modes.reason: Cross-text comparison requires students to hold multiple texts in mind simultaneously, coordinate their respective positions, and synthesise a view of their relationship. This integration — across texts, modes and positions — is the core challenge of the descriptor.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multi-text comparison for ideas and opinion is a transferable academic literacy skill with direct implications for Y9 research tasks and assessments. Advancing students can move beyond binary comparison into mapping a discourse — identifying multiple positions and absences — which is rich and appropriately challenging at Y9.
success_criteria: Student identifies specific ideas or opinions from each text and explains how they compare
Student's comparison goes beyond listing — it explains what the similarities and differences reveal about the texts' positions or purposes
